samples.summary: No test for the "first pending navigation wins" branch when a second guarded push arrives while the dialog is open
samples.evidence: navigation-guard-provider.tsx has an explicit guard `if (!pendingRef.current) { pendingRef.current = run; … }` whose stated purpose is that a second navigation arriving while the prompt is open must not replace the destination the dialog describes. No test in navigation-guard.test.tsx fires a second guarded push while a prompt is open; the closest cases (`drops a prompt the app has already navigated past`, `keeps an open prompt through a query rewrite`) both use *unguarded*/same-page navigations that never reach this branch. If the condition were inverted or removed, the suite stays green while the user is sent to a destination they never clicked after answering "Leave".

samples.summary: Dismissal paths other than the Stay button (Escape, close button, outside click → onOpenChange) are untested
samples.evidence: The provider routes `onOpenChange(false)` to `stay()` and a comment asserts "every way of dismissing this dialog — Escape, the close button, a click outside — also does" [stay]. The tests only click the visible `Stay` and `Leave` buttons (navigation-guard.test.tsx `stays on the page when the user declines`, `replays the exact navigation…`). Nothing asserts that an Escape/outside dismissal clears `pendingRef` rather than replaying the navigation — the failure mode (dismiss ⇒ leave) would silently discard unsent edits.

samples.summary: Multi-guard iteration (one guard declining, a later one blocking) is untested
samples.evidence: `push` loops over `guardsRef.current` and `continue`s past guards that return null. Every test registers exactly one guard (`Editor` mounted once; the `Toggling` test mounts/unmounts a single one). A bug that stopped at the first registered guard — plausible once two editors or an editor plus a future consumer coexist — would leave the suite green and the real guard bypassed.
searchedFor: grep for two <Editor rendered together in tests/components/navigation-guard

samples.summary: The `next === ""` same-page exemption (a `to` carrying only search/hash) has no test
samples.evidence: `leaving` has two exemptions: an empty resolved pathname, and equality with the basenamed current pathname. The test `does not treat a query change on the same page as leaving it` navigates to `/s/doc-1?tab=2`, which resolves to a non-empty pathname and therefore only exercises the equality branch. A `navigate("?tab=2")`-style relative call — the common way a document rewrites its own query — is never exercised, so a regression there would put a modal in front of every query rewrite undetected.
searchedFor: grep for `to="?` and navigate('? in packages/frontend/tests

samples.summary: The PrivateRoute/PublicRoute `replace` change — the invariant the whole guard design rests on — has no test
samples.evidence: The diff adds `replace` to `<Navigate>` in PrivateRoute.tsx and PublicRoute.tsx, justified by the rule that app-issued redirects must not be refusable by the guard (which guards pushes only). A grep of packages/frontend/tests finds PrivateRoute/PublicRoute mentioned only inside navigation-guard.test.tsx's *comments*; there is no test rendering either component. The guard test substitutes a hand-written `<Link to="/login" replace>`, which proves the provider's behaviour but not that these two components actually use replace. If someone drops the flag, the redirect becomes a blockable push and a user with unsent edits can "Stay" in a dead session, with nothing failing.

samples.summary: `guardRef` freshness (guard identity changing without re-registration) is untested
samples.evidence: `useNavigationGuard` registers a stable wrapper `() => guardRef.current()` and updates `guardRef` from an effect keyed on `guard`. No test changes the guard function between registration and fire time — `Harness` passes a constant `blocking`/`passing`, and sync-status-chip-navigation.test.tsx never swaps `hasUnsentEdits` identity after mount. A stale-ref regression would make the guard decide on an outdated document state (either a spurious prompt or, worse, letting unsent edits go silently).

samples.summary: The redirect latch's duration is not pinned: the release test would pass for almost any latch length
samples.evidence: `redirects again after a refused navigation` advances exactly 2000 ms and asserts a second `/login` assignment. It never asserts that the latch is still *held* just before expiry (e.g. advance 1999 ms and expect no second assignment), so a change of REDIRECT_LATCH_MS to 1 ms — which would defeat the burst-dedup purpose during any real async 401 burst — leaves both tests green (test 1 uses fake timers and never advances them). Also, both 401s are issued sequentially, not concurrently, so the concurrent burst the comment describes is not actually reproduced.

samples.summary: `logout({redirect:true})`'s use of the latched `redirectTo("/")` is untested
samples.evidence: tests/api/auth.test.ts only drives `fetchWithAuth`'s 401 path. The other `redirectTo` caller (logout → "/") shares the same module-level latch, so a logout occurring within 2 s of a 401 redirect is silently dropped. No test covers it; searched packages/frontend/tests for `logout(`.

samples.summary: The read-only-viewer and disconnected-reader cases are negative tests that would pass with the guard feature entirely removed
samples.evidence: `never prompts a read-only viewer` renders `SharedHeaderStatus readOnly`, which returns a badge and mounts no chip, so the assertions (`prompted() === false`, `left() === true`) hold regardless of whether useNavigationGuard works at all; same for `does not prompt a disconnected reader with nothing pending`. They are legitimate regression guards but carry no signal about the feature — worth noting only because the file's header presents them as coverage of the guard's reach.
